title: ABRAHAM WAS JUSTIFIED BY FAITH—SO WHY DOES JAMES SAY HE WAS “JUSTIFIED BY WORKS”? THE ANSWER MAY EXPOSE A FAITH YOU NEVER REALIZED WAS DEAD.
paragraphs: ABRAHAM WAS JUSTIFIED BY FAITH—SO WHY DOES JAMES SAY HE WAS “JUSTIFIED BY WORKS”? THE ANSWER MAY EXPOSE A FAITH YOU NEVER REALIZED WAS DEAD.

Paul says Abraham was justified before he worked. James says Abraham was justified by what he did. Both were inspired by the same Holy Spirit. So why do their words sound like a contradiction—and what happens when their answer confronts the way you have been living your Christian life?
There is a kind of faith that knows every Christian phrase but has never truly surrendered.
It knows how to say, “God is good.”
It knows how to raise its hands during worship.
It knows how to quote Scripture when life becomes uncomfortable.
It may even know how to explain salvation by grace.
But when Jesus begins touching the things it refuses to surrender, something changes.
Suddenly, obedience becomes negotiable.
Suddenly, repentance becomes inconvenient.
Suddenly, the same person who confidently says, “I believe in God,” begins living as though God's Word has no authority over the private corners of their life.
And here is the frightening question.
Can someone believe the right things about God and still possess a faith that cannot save?
Before you answer, consider something James wrote that should make every comfortable Christian uncomfortable.
“Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble.” — James 2:19, KJV
Read that again.
Even demons believe that God exists.
They recognize realities about God that many people deny.
But their recognition is not saving trust. It is not love. It is not surrender.
And that brings us to Abraham.
A man whom Scripture calls the friend of God.
A man whose story Paul uses to demonstrate justification by faith apart from works.
Yet the same Abraham becomes James's example when he declares that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.
Was Paul wrong?
Was James correcting him?
Or have we misunderstood what genuine faith actually is?
Because the answer is not merely a theological argument.
It may be the difference between a person who knows how to talk about Jesus and a person whose life is being transformed by Him.
And to understand it, we must return to a man standing beneath a sky full of stars.
Abraham had no impressive spiritual résumé to present before God.
He had no Mosaic Law to boast about. The Law would not be given until centuries later.
He had no perfect record of obedience.
He was an aging man carrying a promise that seemed increasingly impossible.
God had promised him descendants.
Yet Sarah remained childless.
Years passed.
Bodies aged.
Human possibilities diminished.
And still, the promise remained.
Then God brought Abram outside and told him to look toward heaven.
“Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them: and he said unto him, So shall thy seed be.” — Genesis 15:5, KJV
Imagine the silence.
A man with no child of his own looking into a sky filled with more stars than he could count.
Everything he could see in his circumstances contradicted what God had spoken.
But then comes one of the most important sentences in the entire Bible.
“And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness.” — Genesis 15:6, KJV
The Hebrew reads:
וְהֶאֱמִן בַּיהוָה וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ לּוֹ צְדָקָה
Vehe'emin baYHWH, vayachsheveha lo tsedaqah.
“And he believed in the LORD; and He counted it to him as righteousness.”
The Hebrew verb he'emin comes from the root אמן (ʾ-m-n), associated with firmness, reliability, and trust.
In this context, Abraham trusted the LORD and His promise.
The verb vayachsheveha, from חשב (ḥāshav), expresses the act of reckoning, counting, or crediting.
And tsedaqah means righteousness.
Notice what the passage does not say.
It does not say Abraham accumulated enough good deeds to purchase righteousness.
It does not say he became morally flawless.
It does not say God waited until Abraham proved himself worthy.
Abraham believed God, and righteousness was credited to him.
That is the foundation Paul brings into the light in Romans 4.

“For if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; but not before God. For what saith the scripture? Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.” — Romans 4:2–3, KJV
Paul continues:

“Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt. But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.” — Romans 4:4–5, KJV
That last expression is astonishing.
God justifies the ungodly.
Not because ungodliness is acceptable.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because justification is God's gracious gift, received through faith rather than earned as wages for human achievement.
The Greek word Paul uses for “justified” is δικαιόω (dikaioō).
It can refer to declaring someone righteous or vindicating someone, depending on the context.
In Romans 4, Paul's emphasis is unmistakable: God counts righteousness to the believer apart from works as the basis of that verdict.
Paul is not teaching that good works are evil.
He is denying that good works can put God in our debt.
Think about that.
You cannot pray enough to make God owe you salvation.
You cannot give enough money to purchase forgiveness.
You cannot attend enough services to erase your guilt.
You cannot become righteous before God by building a tower of religious accomplishments.
If salvation could be earned, grace would no longer be grace.
And if Christ's sacrifice were unnecessary, why would the Son of God have gone to the cross?
But now comes the verse that appears to overturn everything we have just read.
James 2:24.
“Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only.”
Wait.
Paul says Abraham was justified by faith apart from works.
James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.
And both appeal to Abraham.
If you have ever struggled with this, you are not alone.
The tension is real enough that Christians have debated its interpretation for centuries.
But the first thing we must do is something we often neglect when reading Scripture.
We must allow each biblical writer to finish his argument before forcing his words into a contradiction.
Paul is answering the question of how sinners can be counted righteous before God without earning that standing.
James is confronting people who claim to possess faith while refusing to show mercy or obedience.
Their concerns overlap, but their immediate opponents are different.
Paul confronts confidence in works as the basis of justification.
James confronts confidence in an empty profession of faith.
Paul asks, in effect, “Can your works earn your acceptance before God?”
James asks, “What good is your claimed faith if it produces no response to God or love toward others?”
And James does not leave us guessing about the kind of faith he is confronting.
He writes:
Pay attention to one small expression.
“Though a man say.”
James begins with someone making a claim.
A person says he has faith.
But the question is whether the claim corresponds to a living reality.
In the Greek, James asks:
μὴ δύναται ἡ πίστις σῶσαι αὐτόν;
Mē dynatai hē pistis sōsai auton?
“Can that faith save him?”
The Greek construction anticipates a negative answer. In context, James is challenging the supposed faith of the person who makes a profession but displays no corresponding deeds.
He is not saying that Jesus needs our achievements to complete His saving work.
He is exposing the emptiness of a faith that exists only as a claim.
And James gives an example so ordinary that it becomes painful.
A brother or sister is without adequate clothing and daily food.
Someone sees the need.
Someone speaks religious words.
“Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled.”
But the person gives nothing necessary for the body.
James asks, “What doth it profit?” (James 2:15–16).
Imagine that scene today.
A struggling mother sends a message asking for help.
A brother in Christ admits he has not eaten properly in days.
A family is collapsing under grief.
And someone responds with beautiful Christian language while deliberately refusing the mercy that is within their ability to show.
“God bless you.”
“I'll pray for you.”
“Keep trusting the Lord.”
The words may be true.
Prayer may be deeply appropriate.
But James is confronting a particular hypocrisy: speaking as though we love while withholding practical compassion.
A faith that never reaches the hands has serious questions to answer about what is happening in the heart.
And then James delivers his verdict.
“Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.” — James 2:17, KJV
Not merely immature.
Not simply inconvenient.
Dead.
The Greek word is νεκρά (nekra).
Dead.
James is not describing a living faith that happens to be having a difficult day.
He is warning about a profession of faith that remains barren of the very response faith ought to produce.
And now, perhaps, the question has become uncomfortably personal.
Because it is possible to defend the doctrine of grace while resisting the Lord who gives grace.
It is possible to argue passionately that salvation is not earned while treating obedience as optional.
It is possible to condemn legalism and still use grace as an excuse to protect cherished sin.
But grace was never given to make peace with the sin from which Christ came to save us.
Paul himself asks:
“Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” — Romans 6:1–2, KJV
The apostle who defended justification by faith also insisted that union with Christ changes how believers relate to sin.
So what happened to Abraham?
Why does James point to the offering of Isaac?
Here is where the story becomes extraordinary.
Genesis 15 tells us that Abraham believed God and was counted righteous.
Genesis 22 takes us many years into the future.
Isaac had been born.
The promised son was no longer merely a distant hope.
He was alive.
He had a name.
A face.
A voice Abraham knew.
He was the child through whom God had promised to establish Abraham's descendants.
Then came the test.
God commanded Abraham to offer Isaac.
We must understand this scene carefully.
Genesis presents this as a unique divine test of Abraham, not a general permission for violence or a command for believers to harm their children.
And the narrative does not end with Isaac's death.
God stops Abraham.
Isaac is spared.
A ram is provided.
Yet before that moment of provision, Abraham must confront a devastating question.
Will he trust the God who gave the promise when obedience seems to threaten the very promise he received?
Genesis 22:8 records Abraham saying:
“My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering.”
Hebrews 11:17–19 helps explain Abraham's faith, saying he reasoned that God was able even to raise Isaac from the dead.
Abraham did not know every detail of what God would do.
But he trusted the God whose promise could not fail.
And that trust moved him to obey.
Now listen to James.
“Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar?” — James 2:21, KJV
Then comes the verse that unlocks his argument.
“Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect?” — James 2:22, KJV
In Greek:
ἡ πίστις συνήργει τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ
Hē pistis synērgei tois ergois autou.
“Faith was working together with his works.”
The verb synērgei expresses cooperation or working together.
James continues:
καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἔργων ἡ πίστις ἐτελειώθη
Kai ek tōn ergōn hē pistis eteleiōthē.
“And by the works faith was brought to completion.”
The word eteleiōthē, from teleioō, carries the idea of being brought to its intended completion or maturity.
This does not mean Abraham's faith was previously nonexistent.
James explicitly refers back to Genesis 15:6, where Abraham had already believed God and righteousness had already been credited to him.
Rather, Abraham's obedience in Genesis 22 brought his faith to a decisive expression.
The faith that trusted God's promise under the stars was the faith that obeyed God on the mountain.
The mountain did not manufacture Abraham's faith. It revealed the living character of the faith he already possessed.
And James says Scripture was fulfilled when Abraham's faith came to expression through his obedience (James 2:23).
There is an important theological distinction here.
Christians have historically differed over precisely how to understand James's use of “justified” and how faith, works, and justification relate.
Many Protestant interpreters understand James as speaking of faith being demonstrated or vindicated by works, while Paul speaks of the sinner's being counted righteous before God.
Catholic interpreters emphasize that James also speaks of faith reaching maturity through obedient cooperation with God's grace, not merely being externally demonstrated.
Those differences should not be erased.
Yet the passages establish two truths that Christians should not set against one another: no one can earn God's saving grace, and genuine faith is not indifferent to obedience.
Even the word dikaioō should not be forced to carry a different meaning in every passage simply to make the theological problem disappear.
The context, the chronology of Abraham's life, and the argument of each writer must all be considered.
And James's point becomes especially clear when he compares faith to the human body.
“For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.” — James 2:26, KJV
A body does not become alive by pretending to breathe.
Breathing reveals the presence of life.
In a similar way, acts of obedience do not purchase God's grace, but they belong to the life of faith.
That is why Paul's own words in Ephesians are so important.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
But Paul does not stop there.
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.” — Ephesians 2:10, KJV
Do you see the order?
Grace.
Faith.
Salvation.
A new life that walks in good works.
Good works are not the price of salvation. They are part of the purpose of the new life God gives.
Paul and James are not encouraging us to choose between trusting Christ and following Christ.
They are exposing two different ways of misunderstanding the Gospel.
One person says, “God must accept me because I have done enough.”
Another says, “Because I believe, it does not matter how I live.”
The first makes human achievement the foundation of salvation.
The second empties faith of its living response.
Both miss something essential.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that good people can finally earn their way to heaven.
Nor is it permission to remain comfortably enslaved to sin.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
He saves sinners by grace.
He calls them to repentance.
He reconciles them to God.
And through His Spirit, He begins transforming lives that could never transform themselves.
Now allow that truth to come closer.
Not to the Christian you disagree with online.
Not to the preacher you think needs correction.
Not to the person whose hypocrisy has wounded you.
To you.
To me.
To the private places where nobody else sees what is happening.
What has your faith been producing?
Not how many Bible verses you can quote.
Not how confidently you can debate theology.
Not how impressive your Christian profile looks.
What happens when obedience costs you something?
When telling the truth threatens your reputation?
When forgiving someone means releasing your desire for revenge?
When repentance requires admitting that you were wrong?
When loving your neighbor demands more than a sympathetic comment?
When generosity costs you something you would rather keep?
When following Jesus means surrendering a relationship, a habit, or an ambition that has begun to rule your heart?
These questions are not invitations to earn salvation through moral performance.
They are invitations to examine whether the Christ we profess is also the Lord we are learning to trust.
And if these questions expose something painful, do not run from Jesus.
Run toward Him.
There is a difference between a tender conscience struggling against sin and a hardened heart determined to defend it.
There is a difference between stumbling while following Christ and deciding that following Christ is unnecessary.
A struggling believer may fall.
May weep.
May confess the same weakness with genuine grief.
May need patient discipleship, wise counsel, and the help of the church.
The presence of struggle does not automatically mean the absence of faith.
Sometimes the very grief you feel over your sin is evidence that you no longer want to make peace with it.
Remember Peter.
He boldly declared his loyalty to Jesus.
Then, under pressure, he denied knowing Him.
Three times.
The rooster crowed.
Peter wept bitterly.
What a scandal.
A disciple who had walked with Jesus.
Heard His teaching.
Witnessed His miracles.
And still denied Him when fear took hold.
But Peter's failure was not the final sentence of his story.
The risen Jesus restored him and entrusted him with the care of His sheep (John 21:15–19).
Peter was not restored because his denial had been harmless.
He was restored by the grace of the Savior he had denied.
And that same grace calls sinners away from darkness and back into the light.
Perhaps you have been carrying a private scandal of your own.
A hidden compromise.
A promise you broke.
A season of spiritual indifference.
A pattern you keep excusing.
A relationship damaged by your pride.
A wound you have allowed to turn into bitterness.
You know the right words.
But deep inside, you know something needs to change.
Please hear this.
Jesus does not invite you to manufacture a perfect life before approaching Him. He calls you to come to Him in repentance and faith.
He does not tell the weary to save themselves.
He says:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28, KJV
And the One who welcomes sinners also calls them to follow Him.
Grace is not opposed to obedience.
Grace is opposed to the idea that obedience can make us our own saviors.
The Christian life begins with dependence upon Christ, and it continues in dependence upon Christ.
That is why the Gospel never leaves us admiring Abraham as though he were the ultimate hero.
Abraham's faith points us beyond Abraham.
To Jesus.
Abraham trusted God's promise of a son.
Jesus is the promised offspring through whom God's blessing reaches the nations, as Paul explains in Galatians 3:16.
Abraham faced a test involving his beloved son.
At Calvary, the Father truly gave His beloved Son for the salvation of sinners.
Isaac was spared.
Jesus willingly laid down His life.
The comparison is not identical in every detail, but the larger biblical story directs our attention to the sacrifice and provision of God.
And unlike Abraham, whose obedience was imperfect, Jesus obeyed the Father without sin.
Philippians 2:8 says He became “obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.”
Our hope does not rest in how closely we can imitate Abraham.
Our hope rests in the crucified and risen Christ.
The One who fulfilled righteousness.
The One who bore sin.
The One who conquered death.
The One who gives forgiveness and new life to those who trust Him.
And here is the beautiful irony.
The more deeply you understand that salvation is a gift, the less you should want to treat obedience as a burden you can safely ignore.
Love begins to change what duty alone could never accomplish.
You no longer obey to force God to love you.
You learn to obey because, in Christ, you have encountered a love you could never earn.
You begin to forgive because you have been forgiven.
You begin to show mercy because mercy has reached you.
You begin to tell the truth because you belong to the One who is truth.
You begin to give because you know everything you possess is ultimately entrusted to you.
Not perfectly.
Not without struggle.
But genuinely.
And when you fail, you return to the Savior rather than hiding behind a religious performance.
That is the beauty of living faith.
It does not boast, “Look how righteous I have made myself.”
It confesses, “Look how merciful Jesus has been to me.”
And now we must confront another question.
It means generosity matters.
Not because money can purchase forgiveness.
Not because a ministry can sell God's blessing.
But because those who have received grace are invited to become generous stewards of what God has entrusted to them.
Paul writes:
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly. Not of necessity.
Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and motivated by love—not fear, manipulation, or pressure.
If the teaching of Abraham and James moves you to support Gospel ministry, let it be an expression of gratitude to Christ, not an attempt to earn His favor.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, return to Jesus, resist compromise, or find hope in a difficult season, your partnership can help this ministry continue reaching others.
There is no spiritual price tag attached to the Gospel.
And there never will be.
But faithful ministry does involve real work, real resources, and real people who need to be reached.
Behind every article is the possibility that someone who has quietly drifted from God may read a sentence that brings them back to Scripture.
Someone battling despair may discover a reason to keep seeking Christ.
Someone who thought Christianity was merely a collection of rules may finally understand the grace of Jesus.
Someone who has never understood the relationship between faith and works may stop trying to earn salvation and begin trusting the Savior.
These resources can serve as reminders of biblical truth and opportunities to encourage others. They are not spiritual rewards or measures of anyone's faith.
Because spiritual growth should never be reduced to what someone can afford.
But there is another way you can help today that costs nothing.
Not merely to increase its reach.
Someone may be hiding behind the language of grace while avoiding repentance.
Someone may be exhausted from trying to earn a salvation that Jesus offers freely.
Someone may be a wounded believer who needs to hear that failure does not have to be the end of the story.
And someone may have abandoned Christianity because they thought Paul and James contradicted each other.
One thoughtful share could put these Scriptures before a person who would never have searched for them.
And before you leave, I want to ask you something that matters more than winning a theological debate.
What is one area of your life where you know God is calling you to move beyond words and trust Him through obedience?
Perhaps it is forgiveness.
Perhaps repentance.
Perhaps making something right.
Perhaps showing mercy.
Perhaps finally trusting Jesus instead of your own religious efforts.
You do not have to expose private details to strangers. God already knows what is hidden in your heart.

And if you have a testimony of how Jesus brought you from religious performance into genuine trust, consider sharing it. Someone else may need the encouragement of knowing that grace is still changing lives.
Not to prove that your faith is alive.
Not to impress God.
Not to purchase a blessing.
But freely, as an act of Christian generosity, if you believe the work is faithful and worth supporting.
Because the very passage we have studied warns us against confusing outward action with the heart of faith.
A person can give money without trusting Christ.
A person can even do impressive religious works while remaining spiritually empty.
So the question is not whether you have clicked the right button, donated the right amount, or performed enough visible deeds.
The question is whether your confidence rests in Jesus Christ—and whether that faith is beginning to bear the fruit of His grace.
Return, for a moment, to Abraham beneath the stars.
An old man.
An impossible promise.
A God who could be trusted.
Then remember Abraham on the mountain.
Years had passed.
The circumstances had changed.
The test had become costly.
But the God he trusted was still the same.
Faith had not remained a sentence on Abraham's lips.
It had shaped the direction of his life.
And that is why Paul and James belong together.
Paul will not let you boast that your works have earned righteousness.
James will not let you boast that an empty claim is living faith.
Paul directs the sinner away from self-righteousness.
James directs the professing believer away from self-deception.
Both drive us toward the necessity of genuine faith.
And genuine Christian faith finds its object, its hope, and its salvation in Jesus Christ.
So do not leave this article asking only, “Which apostle was right?”
Ask instead:
“Lord Jesus, am I trusting You—or merely trusting the fact that I know things about You?”
“Have I mistaken Christian language for Christian life?”
“Am I trying to earn what You have freely given?”
“Or am I using Your grace to excuse what You are calling me to surrender?”
And if the answer hurts, remember Peter.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that the Savior who calls sinners to repentance is also the Savior who receives those who come to Him.
You do not need to rewrite your past before approaching Jesus.
You need the mercy of the One who died and rose again.
Because the Gospel does not end with the scandal of human failure.
It announces the grace of divine redemption.
The final word over the repentant believer is not the worst thing they have done.
It is the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the most unforgettable truth of Abraham's story is this:
The faith that was counted as righteousness beneath the stars was the faith that walked in obedience upon the mountain.
Not two competing salvations.
Not two opposing Gospels.
But a living trust in the God who keeps His promises.
So come to Christ with empty hands.
Receive His grace through faith.
And by that same grace, learn to follow Him with your whole life.
Because the greatest tragedy is not discovering that your faith has been weak—it is spending your life defending a faith you have never allowed Jesus to bring into the light.
